P R A C T I C E M AT E R I A L - C H A S S I S P R O G R A M


Chassis Pop Quizzes
11 quizzes - one per course - covering all 43 modules in the chassis completion sheet.

Name:                                                          Date:

How to use: Take one quiz after finishing a course. Circle the best answer (A-D), then check your
answers in the separate Answer Key section at the back of this pack. Review the module named under
any question you missed. Untimed on the first run; repeat the quiz later and aim for 9/10 or better before
moving on.
Answer keys are separate: all keys are grouped at the back, after Quiz 11, so the quizzes can be
printed and taken without the answers.

C O U R S E S I N T H I S PA C K

1. Course 1 - Tire and Rim Essentials (4 modules, 10 questions)
2. Course 2 - Best Practice Tire Fitment (3 modules, 10 questions)
3. Course 3 - Introducing Suspension Components (6 modules, 10 questions)
4. Course 4 - Understanding Suspension Systems (7 modules, 10 questions)
5. Course 5 - Advanced Suspension Technology (2 modules, 10 questions)
6. Course 6 - Complete Steering Systems (5 modules, 10 questions)
7. Course 7 - Mastering Wheel Alignments (1 module, 10 questions)
8. Course 8 - Braking System Essentials (6 modules, 10 questions)
9. Course 9 - Advanced Braking System (2 modules, 10 questions)
10. Course 10 - ABS Operations and Testing (4 modules, 10 questions)
11. Course 11 - Park Brake Technology (3 modules, 10 questions)

Course 1: Tire and Rim Essentials
Name:                                           Date:                                      Score: ___ / 10

  MODULES COVERED (4)
     Tire Technology
     Tread and Rim Technology
     Run Flat Tires
     Tire Pressure Monitoring


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.

1. What does the 'R' in a tire size such as 225/65R17 mean? [TIRE TECHNOLOGY]
   A. Radial construction
   B. Run flat rated
   C. Reinforced sidewall
   D. Rear fitment only

2. In the size 225/65R17, what does 65 represent? [TIRE TECHNOLOGY]
   A. The tread width in millimetres
   B. The aspect ratio - sidewall height as 65% of width
   C. The load index
   D. The speed rating

3. A tire's DOT date code ends in '24' for its last two digits. What does that indicate? [TIRE
TECHNOLOGY]

   A. The tire's speed rating
   B. The week it was made
   C. The year it was manufactured - 2024
   D. The maximum pressure in bar

4. What is the main purpose of the tread pattern's circumferential grooves? [TREAD AND RIM
TECHNOLOGY]

   A. To increase sidewall stiffness
   B. To make the tire quieter only
   C. To add weight
   D. To channel water away and resist hydroplaning
5. What does a rim's offset describe? [TREAD AND RIM TECHNOLOGY]
   A. The distance between the mounting surface and the rim centreline
   B. The diameter of the centre bore only
   C. The number of lug holes
   D. The width of the tire bead




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                Course 1 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 1 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 1: Tire and Rim Essentials - Questions 6-10
6. Tread wear bars level with the tread surface indicate the tire is: [TREAD AND RIM TECHNOLOGY]
   A. Brand new
   B. At or near the legal minimum tread depth and due for replacement
   C. Overinflated
   D. In need of balancing only

7. How does a self-supporting run flat tire keep working after a puncture? [RUN FLAT TIRES]
   A. It seals itself with liquid inside
   B. Its reinforced, stiff sidewalls support the vehicle load with no air pressure
   C. It has a solid rubber core
   D. The rim locks the bead so air cannot escape

8. After driving on a deflated run flat tire, best practice is generally to: [RUN FLAT TIRES]
   A. Repair it like any standard tire in all cases
   B. Drive indefinitely if it still holds shape
   C. Replace it, because internal sidewall damage may not be visible
   D. Increase its pressure above maximum

9. A direct TPMS system measures pressure using: [TIRE PRESSURE MONITORING]
   A. The ABS wheel speed sensors
   B. Sensors mounted inside each wheel/tire assembly
   C. Engine vacuum
   D. The brake fluid level sensor

10. After rotating tires on a vehicle with direct TPMS, what may be required? [TIRE PRESSURE
MONITORING]

   A. Nothing, ever
   B. A relearn procedure so the system knows each sensor's new position
   C. Removal of all sensors
   D. Deflating every tire to zero

Course 2: Best Practice Tire Fitment
Name:                                            Date:                                     Score: ___ / 10

  MODULES COVERED (3)
     Best Practice Standard Wheel Balancing
     Best Practice Standard Tire Strip and Fitment
     Best Practice Low Profile / Run Flat Tire Strip and Fit


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.

1. Static imbalance in a wheel assembly will most likely cause: [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD WHEEL
BALANCING]

   A. A side-to-side steering shimmy only
   B. A vertical hop or bounce as speed increases
   C. A constant pull to one side
   D. Excessive camber wear only

2. Before balancing a wheel, best practice is to: [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD WHEEL BALANCING]
   A. Add extra weights to compensate for dirt
   B. Remove old weights and clean the rim and tire
   C. Balance with the tire deflated
   D. Spin it with the valve cap removed only

3. A balancer asks for weights in two planes. This corrects: [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD WHEEL
BALANCING]

   A. Static imbalance only
   B. Runout
   C. Dynamic (couple) imbalance that causes wobble
   D. Bead seating

4. When stripping a tire from a rim, the bead must first be: [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND
FITMENT]

   A. Cut with a knife
   B. Fully inflated
   C. Pushed off the bead seat (broken) on both sides
   D. Heated until soft

5. Why is lubricant applied to tire beads during fitment? [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND
FITMENT]

   A. To glue the bead to the rim
   B. To help the bead slide over the rim and seat without damage
   C. To balance the wheel
   D. To stop the tire rotating on the rim permanently




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                Course 2 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 2 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 2: Best Practice Tire Fitment - Questions 6-10
6. When seating beads during inflation, the technician should: [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD TIRE STRIP
AND FITMENT]

   A. Stand directly over the tire with no restraint
   B. Exceed maximum pressure until the beads pop, whatever it takes
   C. Use a safety cage or clip-on chuck and stay within the stated maximum seating pressure
   D. Remove the valve core permanently

7. The yellow dot on many new tires marks: [BEST PRACTICE STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND FITMENT]
   A. The heaviest point
   B. The lightest point, often aligned with the valve stem
   C. A puncture repair
   D. The maximum speed point

8. Low profile and run flat tires are harder to strip and fit mainly because: [BEST PRACTICE LOW
PROFILE / RUN FLAT TIRE STRIP AND FIT]

   A. They are much heavier
   B. Their stiff, short sidewalls flex far less over the rim
   C. They use a different valve type only
   D. They cannot be lubricated

9. When fitting a run flat tire, the TPMS sensor is at risk during: [BEST PRACTICE LOW PROFILE / RUN
FLAT TIRE STRIP AND FIT]

   A. Balancing only
   B. Bead breaking and lever work near the valve/sensor position
   C. Final torque of the wheel nuts
   D. Road testing

10. Using press/roller helper arms on the changer for a stiff low profile tire helps to: [BEST
PRACTICE LOW PROFILE / RUN FLAT TIRE STRIP AND FIT]

   A. Inflate the tire faster
   B. Keep the bead in the drop centre so it can pass over the flange without overstretching
   C. Remove the need for lubricant
   D. Measure tread depth

Course 3: Introducing Suspension Components
Name:                                            Date:                                     Score: ___ / 10

  MODULES COVERED (6)
     Suspension System Principles
     Suspension Component Springs
     Suspension Component Shocks
     Suspension Component Linkage
     Suspension Component Anti-Roll
     Suspension Component Bushes


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.
1. Sprung mass refers to: [SUSPENSION SYSTEM PRINCIPLES]
   A. Only the wheels and tires
   B. The mass supported by the springs, such as body and engine
   C. The mass below the springs only
   D. Fuel in the tank only

2. Reducing unsprung mass generally helps the tire to: [SUSPENSION SYSTEM PRINCIPLES]
   A. Wear faster
   B. Stay in contact with the road over bumps
   C. Increase body roll
   D. Raise the ride height

3. A coil spring's rate describes: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT SPRINGS]
   A. Its colour coding only
   B. How much force is needed to compress it a given distance
   C. Its maximum extended length
   D. The number of coils only

4. A broken or sagging spring will most directly affect: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT SPRINGS]
   A. Ride height and wheel alignment angles
   B. Engine power
   C. Brake fluid level
   D. Tire pressure readings

5. The shock absorber's job is to: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT SHOCKS]
   A. Carry the vehicle's weight
   B. Hold the wheel alignment
   C. Control (damp) spring oscillation after a bump
   D. Replace the spring




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                Course 3 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 3 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 3: Introducing Suspension Components - Questions 6-
10
6. A worn shock absorber will most likely cause: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT SHOCKS]
   A. A single bounce then stop
   B. Continued bouncing after a bump and uneven (cupped) tire wear
   C. No change in handling
   D. A lower engine idle

7. Excess play in a suspension ball joint is best checked by: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT LINKAGE]
   A. Looking at it only
   B. Loading/unloading the joint as directed and measuring movement against specification
   C. Checking tire pressure
   D. Turning the steering to full lock only

8. Control arms locate the wheel by: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT LINKAGE]
   A. Holding brake fluid
   B. Connecting the knuckle/hub to the body or subframe and controlling its movement path
   C. Driving the wheel
   D. Cooling the brakes

9. An anti-roll (stabilizer) bar reduces body roll by: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT ANTI-ROLL]
   A. Stiffening both springs permanently
   B. Twisting to transfer load between the two sides when they move differently
   C. Locking the steering
   D. Lowering the centre of gravity

10. Worn suspension bushes commonly cause: [SUSPENSION COMPONENT BUSHES]
   A. Higher fuel pressure
   B. Clunks over bumps, vague handling and uneven tire wear
   C. A brighter headlamp beam
   D. Faster wheel speed sensor signals

     MACPERSON Strut Inspection Procedures
     Torsion Bar System Components and Operations

     Double Wishbone System Components and Operations
     Double Wishbone Inspection Procedures
     Electronic Kinetic Dynamic Suspension


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.
1. In a MacPherson strut system, the strut itself: [MACPERSON STRUT SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND
OPERATION]

   A. Is only a shock absorber and carries no load path
   B. Forms part of the steering/suspension location, with the spring around it and a top mount to the body
   C. Is mounted to the exhaust
   D. Replaces the wheel bearing

2. The strut top mount bearing allows: [MACPERSON STRUT SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND OPERATION]
   A. The wheel to change diameter
   B. The strut to rotate as the steering turns
   C. The spring to detach
   D. The brake disc to float

3. Before removing a strut spring, the spring must be: [MACPERSON STRUT INSPECTION PROCEDURES]
   A. Cut in half
   B. Heated
   C. Safely compressed with a proper spring compressor
   D. Left fully loaded while bolts are removed

4. Oil misting/leaking from a strut body and a failed bounce test indicate: [MACPERSON STRUT
INSPECTION PROCEDURES]

   A. A normal strut
   B. A worn strut needing replacement, normally in axle pairs
   C. Only a tire fault
   D. A steering rack fault only

5. A torsion bar spring works by: [TORSION BAR SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]
   A. Compressing like a coil
   B. Twisting along its length as the control arm moves
   C. Bending a leaf pack
   D. Trapping air




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                   Course 4 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 4 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 4: Understanding Suspension Systems - Questions 6-
10
6. Ride height on a torsion bar system is commonly adjusted by: [TORSION BAR SYSTEM
COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]

   A. Changing tire size
   B. Turning the anchor adjuster bolt to add or reduce bar preload (twist)
   C. Replacing the shocks
   D. Adding wheel weights

7. During torsion bar inspection, cracking or heavy corrosion on the bar is serious because:
[TORSION BAR INSPECTION PROCEDURES]

   A. It only affects paint finish
   B. A fatigued bar can snap suddenly under its torsional load
   C. It changes tire pressure
   D. It makes the bar quieter

8. A double wishbone system uses: [DOUBLE WISHBONE SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]
   A. One arm per wheel
   B. Upper and lower arms, which control camber change through travel
   C. A solid beam only
   D. A torsion beam only
9. Play found at the wheel on a double wishbone system could come from: [DOUBLE WISHBONE
INSPECTION PROCEDURES]

   A. Ball joints, arm bushes or the wheel bearing - each must be isolated to find the source
   B. The brake fluid
   C. The tire valve
   D. The spring colour

10. An electronic kinetic dynamic suspension system improves both roll control and off-road
articulation by: [ELECTRONIC KINETIC DYNAMIC SUSPENSION]
   A. Fitting stiffer bars permanently
   B. Hydraulically/electronically controlling the anti-roll bars so they can stiffen on road and free up off road
   C. Removing the anti-roll bars
   D. Locking all dampers solid

  MODULES COVERED (2)
     Air Suspension Overview
     Suspension Components Active Shocks


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.
1. In an air suspension system, the steel coil spring is replaced by: [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]
   A. A solid rubber block
   B. A flexible air spring (air bag) filled with compressed air
   C. A torsion bar
   D. A leaf spring

2. Ride height in an air suspension system is monitored by: [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]
   A. Height sensors linked to the control module, which adds or vents air to correct height
   B. The driver guessing
   C. Tire pressure sensors only
   D. The speedometer only

3. The air compressor in this system primarily: [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]
   A. Cools the engine
   B. Supplies pressurised air to fill the springs/reservoir when height must rise
   C. Pumps brake fluid
   D. Charges the battery

4. A vehicle that sags at one corner overnight most likely has: [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]
   A. A faulty headlamp
   B. An air leak at that corner's spring, line or valve
   C. Too much fuel
   D. A worn wiper blade

5. Before jacking or lifting an air suspension vehicle, best practice is to: [AIR SUSPENSION
OVERVIEW]

   A. Ignore the system completely
   B. Follow the maker's procedure - often selecting jack/service mode or disabling the system
   C. Deflate the tires
   D. Remove the battery from the car and discard it




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                    Course 5 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 5 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 5: Advanced Suspension Technology - Questions 6-10
6. A dryer unit is fitted in many air suspension systems to: [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]
   A. Dry the brake discs
   B. Remove moisture from the compressed air to protect valves and springs
   C. Dry the cabin air only
   D. Filter engine oil

7. An active/adaptive shock absorber changes its damping by: [SUSPENSION COMPONENTS ACTIVE
SHOCKS]

   A. The driver swapping the shocks
   B. Varying oil flow through an electrically controlled valve (or changing fluid properties) in response to
   module commands
   C. Changing spring rate
   D. Moving the wheel

8. Inputs an active suspension module commonly uses include: [SUSPENSION COMPONENTS ACTIVE
SHOCKS]

   A. Radio volume
   B. Steering angle, wheel/body movement, vehicle speed and drive mode
   C. Fuel brand
   D. Paint colour

9. In a firmer sport drive mode, active shocks will generally: [SUSPENSION COMPONENTS ACTIVE
SHOCKS]

   A. Reduce damping to minimum
   B. Increase damping to limit body roll, pitch and dive
   C. Turn off completely
   D. Lock the springs solid
10. A failed active shock electrical connector will most likely: [SUSPENSION COMPONENTS ACTIVE
SHOCKS]

   A. Have no effect at all
   B. Set a fault code and cause that damper to default to a fixed (failsafe) damping setting
   C. Increase engine power
   D. Change tire size

Course 6: Complete Steering Systems
Name:                                             Date:                                             Score: ___ / 10

  MODULES COVERED (5)
     Manual Steering Principles
     Hydraulic Power Steering
     Electro Hydraulic Power Steering
     Electric Power Steering
     Electric Power Steering Diagnostics


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.
1. In a manual rack and pinion, turning the steering wheel moves the rack by: [MANUAL STEERING
PRINCIPLES]

   A. A hydraulic pump
   B. The pinion gear meshing with teeth on the rack, converting rotation into linear movement
   C. A belt drive
   D. An electric motor

2. Steering ratio describes: [MANUAL STEERING PRINCIPLES]
   A. Tire pressure front to rear
   B. How many degrees the steering wheel turns for a given degree of road wheel movement
   C. The size of the steering wheel
   D. Power steering fluid capacity

3. In hydraulic power steering, assistance comes from: [HYDRAULIC POWER STEERING]
   A. Engine vacuum only
   B. Pressurised fluid from an engine-driven pump acting in the rack or box
   C. An electric motor on the column
   D. The alternator

4. Heavy steering with whining noise from the pump most often indicates: [HYDRAULIC POWER
STEERING]

   A. Too much fluid
   B. Low fluid level or air in the system (aeration)
   C. A new belt
   D. Normal operation in all cases

5. A rotary control valve in the steering gear works to: [HYDRAULIC POWER STEERING]
   A. Direct pressurised fluid to the correct side of the piston in proportion to steering effort
   B. Filter the fluid
   C. Cool the fluid
   D. Drive the pump




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                         Course 6 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 6 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 6: Complete Steering Systems - Questions 6-10
6. Electro hydraulic power steering differs from conventional hydraulic steering because:
[ELECTRO HYDRAULIC POWER STEERING]

   A. It uses no fluid
   B. Its pump is driven by an electric motor rather than directly by the engine
   C. It has no rack
   D. It only works when parked

7. One advantage of electro hydraulic steering is that the module can: [ELECTRO HYDRAULIC POWER
STEERING]

   A. Vary pump speed with demand - running slower when no assistance is needed, saving energy
   B. Remove the steering wheel
   C. Change tire tread
   D. Eliminate alignment checks

8. In electric power steering (EPS), assistance is provided by: [ELECTRIC POWER STEERING]
   A. Hydraulic fluid
   B. An electric motor acting on the column, pinion or rack
   C. Engine vacuum
   D. A second steering box

9. The steering torque sensor in an EPS system measures: [ELECTRIC POWER STEERING]
   A. Road speed
   B. How hard and in which direction the driver is turning the wheel
   C. Tire temperature
   D. Brake pressure

10. After replacing an EPS component or performing an alignment, a scan tool procedure often
required is: [ELECTRIC POWER STEERING DIAGNOSTICS]
   A. Deleting all keys
   B. Steering angle sensor calibration / zero point relearn
   C. Draining the fuel tank
   D. Resetting the radio

Course 7: Mastering Wheel Alignments
Name:                                              Date:                                       Score: ___ / 10

  MODULES COVERED (1)
     Understanding Steering Angles


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.

1. Camber is defined as: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. The forward tilt of the steering axis
   B. The inward or outward tilt of the top of the wheel when viewed from the front
   C. The difference in angle between the two front wheels in a turn
   D. The direction the rear wheels point

2. Excessive negative camber will wear the tire mainly on its: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. Outer shoulder
   B. Centre
   C. Inner shoulder
   D. Both shoulders equally

3. Caster mainly affects: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. Tire pressure
   B. Steering returnability and straight-line stability
   C. Brake bias
   D. Turning radius only

4. Toe is best described as: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. The tilt of the wheel from the front
   B. Whether the fronts of the tires point in toward each other, out, or straight ahead, viewed from above
   C. The height of the vehicle
   D. The angle of the driveshaft

5. Excess toe-in or toe-out will most quickly cause: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. Engine wear
   B. Feathered/scuffed tire tread wear and possible steering pull or wander
   C. Brake fade
   D. A dead battery




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                    Course 7 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 7 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 7: Mastering Wheel Alignments - Questions 6-10
6. Steering axis inclination (SAI) is: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. Adjustable on every car with shims
   B. The inward tilt of the steering axis from vertical, viewed from the front, largely set by design
   C. The same as toe
   D. Measured only on the rear axle

7. Included angle is the combination of: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. Camber plus toe
   B. SAI plus camber
   C. Caster plus toe
   D. Ride height plus camber

8. Thrust angle describes: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. The angle of the steering wheel only
   B. The direction the rear axle points compared with the vehicle centreline
   C. The pitch of the body under braking
   D. The angle of the front bumper

9. Ackermann (toe-out on turns) allows: [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]
   A. Both front wheels to turn at exactly the same angle
   B. The inside wheel to turn more sharply than the outside wheel, because it follows a smaller radius
   C. The rear wheels to steer
   D. The steering wheel to lock

10. Before measuring any alignment angles, the technician should first check: [UNDERSTANDING
STEERING ANGLES]

   A. Radio presets
   B. Ride height, tire pressures and sizes, and for worn or loose steering/suspension parts
   C. Fuel level only and nothing else
   D. Headlamp aim only

  MODULES COVERED (6)
     Automotive Braking Principles
     Understanding Brake Fluid
     Brake Master Cylinder Operation
     Disc Brake Systems
     Drum Brake Systems Components and Operations
     Drum Brake Systems Configuration and Maintenance


Circle the best answer for each question. Answer key: see the separate Answer Key section at the back.

1. Brakes slow the vehicle by converting kinetic energy into: [AUTOMOTIVE BRAKING PRINCIPLES]
   A. Electrical energy
   B. Heat through friction
   C. Fuel
   D. Sound only

2. Hydraulic brake force works on Pascal's principle, which states: [AUTOMOTIVE BRAKING
PRINCIPLES]

   A. Pressure in a confined fluid acts only downward
   B. Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions
   C. Fluid pressure disappears in long lines
   D. Air in the lines improves pressure

3. Brake fluid must be hygroscopic-managed because it: [UNDERSTANDING BRAKE FLUID]
   A. Repels all water forever
   B. Absorbs moisture over time, which lowers its boiling point and can corrode parts
   C. Is the same as engine oil
   D. Never needs changing

4. Mixing or using the wrong specification of brake fluid can cause: [UNDERSTANDING BRAKE FLUID]
   A. Better braking in all cases
   B. Seal swelling/damage and reduced performance - only the specified DOT grade should be used
   C. No possible harm
   D. The brakes to self-bleed

5. A tandem master cylinder has two separate hydraulic circuits so that: [BRAKE MASTER CYLINDER
OPERATION]

   A. The brakes work twice as fast
   B. If one circuit fails, the other can still provide braking on its wheels
   C. Only the front brakes work
   D. Fluid never needs topping up




Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                  Course 8 - Questions 1-5
COURSE 8 - POP QUIZ, CONTINUED

Course 8: Braking System Essentials - Questions 6-10
6. The compensating (bypass) port in the master cylinder allows: [BRAKE MASTER CYLINDER
OPERATION]

   A. Air into the system
   B. Fluid to return to the reservoir and release pressure when the pedal is released, and make up for pad
   wear
   C. The pedal to lock down
   D. Exhaust gas into the fluid

7. In a disc brake, braking force is produced when: [DISC BRAKE SYSTEMS]
   A. Shoes expand into a drum
   B. The caliper squeezes pads against both faces of a rotating disc
   C. Fluid boils
   D. The handbrake cable pulls only

8. A floating caliper moves on its slides so that: [DISC BRAKE SYSTEMS]
   A. Only the inner pad ever touches the disc
   B. Both pads apply evenly - piston pushes one pad and the caliper reaction pulls the other in
   C. The disc can wobble freely
   D. The wheel can be removed without tools

9. In a drum brake, the shoes are forced outward against the drum by: [DRUM BRAKE SYSTEMS
COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]

   A. The return springs
   B. The wheel cylinder pistons
   C. The adjuster only
   D. Centrifugal force

10. Self-adjusters on drum brakes maintain: [DRUM BRAKE SYSTEMS CONFIGURATION AND
MAINTENANCE]

   A. Tire pressure
   B. Correct shoe-to-drum clearance as the linings wear
   C. Brake fluid level
   D. Disc thickness

A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 1 O F 11

Quiz 1: Tire and Rim Essentials - Answer Key
1. A - The R stands for radial construction, where the ply cords run radially across the tire. [TIRE TECHNOLOGY]

2. B - 65 is the aspect ratio: sidewall height is 65 percent of the section width. [TIRE TECHNOLOGY]

3. C - The last two digits of the DOT code are the year of manufacture. [TIRE TECHNOLOGY]

4. D - Circumferential grooves evacuate water from the contact patch to maintain grip in the wet. [TREAD AND RIM
TECHNOLOGY]

5. A - Offset is the distance from the hub mounting surface to the rim's centreline. [TREAD AND RIM TECHNOLOGY]

6. B - Wear bars flush with the tread mean the tread is worn to its minimum usable depth. [TREAD AND RIM
TECHNOLOGY]

7. B - Run flat sidewalls are reinforced so they can carry the load for a limited distance at reduced speed with zero
pressure. [RUN FLAT TIRES]
8. C - Run flats driven deflated can suffer hidden structural damage, so replacement is the safe best practice. [RUN
FLAT TIRES]

9. B - Direct TPMS uses a pressure sensor inside each wheel that transmits actual pressure. [TIRE PRESSURE
MONITORING]

10. B - A relearn matches each sensor ID to its new wheel position so the display shows the correct corner. [TIRE
PRESSURE MONITORING]

A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 2 O F 11

Quiz 2: Best Practice Tire Fitment - Answer Key
1. B - Static imbalance makes the heavy spot lift and drop each revolution, causing a hop. [BEST PRACTICE
STANDARD WHEEL BALANCING]

2. B - Old weights and dirt change the result, so the assembly is cleaned and old weights removed first. [BEST
PRACTICE STANDARD WHEEL BALANCING]

3. C - Two-plane balancing corrects dynamic imbalance, which produces a wobbling couple force. [BEST PRACTICE
STANDARD WHEEL BALANCING]

4. C - Both beads must be broken free from their seats before the tire can be levered off safely. [BEST PRACTICE
STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND FITMENT]

5. B - Bead lubricant reduces friction so the bead passes over the rim flange and seats evenly. [BEST PRACTICE
STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND FITMENT]

6. C - Bead seating is done with restraint/clip-on chuck and never above the maker's maximum seating pressure.
[BEST PRACTICE STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND FITMENT]

7. B - The yellow dot marks the lightest point and is commonly aligned with the valve stem. [BEST PRACTICE
STANDARD TIRE STRIP AND FITMENT]

8. B - Short, stiff sidewalls resist the flexing needed to clear the rim flange, so technique and machine helpers
matter. [BEST PRACTICE LOW PROFILE / RUN FLAT TIRE STRIP AND FIT]

9. B - Levers and the bead passing the sensor area can crack the sensor if its position is ignored. [BEST PRACTICE
LOW PROFILE / RUN FLAT TIRE STRIP AND FIT]

10. B - Helpers hold the bead in the drop centre, giving the slack needed to fit a stiff tire safely. [BEST PRACTICE
LOW PROFILE / RUN FLAT TIRE STRIP AND FIT]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                              Answer Key - Quiz 2
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 3 O F 11

Quiz 3: Introducing Suspension Components - Answer Key
1. B - Sprung mass is everything the springs carry; wheels and brakes below the springs are unsprung mass.
[SUSPENSION SYSTEM PRINCIPLES]

2. B - Lighter unsprung parts follow road bumps more easily, keeping the tire planted. [SUSPENSION SYSTEM
PRINCIPLES]

3. B - Spring rate is force per unit of deflection, for example newtons per millimetre. [SUSPENSION COMPONENT
SPRINGS]

4. A - A weak spring lowers ride height, which changes camber and other alignment angles. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENT SPRINGS]

5. C - Shocks damp spring movement by converting motion into heat in the oil; springs carry the load.
[SUSPENSION COMPONENT SHOCKS]

6. B - Weak damping lets the wheel keep bouncing, which cups the tread and hurts control. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENT SHOCKS]

7. B - Ball joint wear is measured as movement under the maker's specified load condition. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENT LINKAGE]

8. B - Arms and links position the hub and define how it moves through suspension travel. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENT LINKAGE]

9. B - The bar resists one side compressing more than the other, which is what body roll is. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENT ANTI-ROLL]

10. B - Perished or split bushes allow excess movement, causing noise, play and alignment shift under load.
[SUSPENSION COMPONENT BUSHES]

A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 4 O F 11

Quiz 4: Understanding Suspension Systems - Answer Key
1. B - The strut is a structural member: it locates the wheel, carries the spring, and steers with the knuckle.
[MACPERSON STRUT SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND OPERATION]

2. B - The top bearing lets the whole strut assembly pivot smoothly during steering. [MACPERSON STRUT SYSTEM
COMPONENTS AND OPERATION]

3. C - A loaded coil spring stores dangerous energy and must be compressed with the correct tool first.
[MACPERSON STRUT INSPECTION PROCEDURES]

4. B - Leakage plus poor damping means the strut is worn; struts are normally renewed in pairs. [MACPERSON
STRUT INSPECTION PROCEDURES]

5. B - The bar twists to provide spring force, anchored at one end and driven by the arm at the other. [TORSION
BAR SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]

6. B - The adjuster changes the bar's preload angle, raising or lowering ride height. [TORSION BAR SYSTEM
COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]

7. B - The bar works under high torsional stress, so cracks can lead to sudden failure. [TORSION BAR INSPECTION
PROCEDURES]

8. B - Two arms of different effective length control how camber changes as the wheel rises and falls. [DOUBLE
WISHBONE SYSTEM COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]

9. A - Several joints can produce play, so each is checked separately under the right load. [DOUBLE WISHBONE
INSPECTION PROCEDURES]

10. B - It varies anti-roll bar resistance: stiff against roll on road, relaxed for wheel articulation off road.
[ELECTRONIC KINETIC DYNAMIC SUSPENSION]

Quiz 5: Advanced Suspension Technology - Answer Key
1. B - Air springs use pressurised air in a rubber bellows to support the load. [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]

2. A - Height sensors report body position and the module commands the compressor or exhaust valve to correct it.
[AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]

3. B - The compressor provides the air needed to inflate the springs and restore ride height. [AIR SUSPENSION
OVERVIEW]

4. B - A slow overnight drop at one corner points to an air leak in that corner's circuit. [AIR SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]

5. B - Service/jack mode stops the system levelling while lifted, which could move the vehicle or damage parts. [AIR
SUSPENSION OVERVIEW]

6. B - Removing moisture prevents corrosion and freezing inside valves and air lines. [AIR SUSPENSION
OVERVIEW]

7. B - Adaptive dampers vary their valving electrically so damping can change in milliseconds. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENTS ACTIVE SHOCKS]

8. B - The module blends sensor inputs and the selected mode to set damping for each corner. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENTS ACTIVE SHOCKS]

9. B - Sport mode firms damping to control body movement more tightly. [SUSPENSION COMPONENTS ACTIVE
SHOCKS]

10. B - With no control signal the damper defaults to a preset rate and the system logs a fault. [SUSPENSION
COMPONENTS ACTIVE SHOCKS]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                           Answer Key - Quiz 5
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 6 O F 11

Quiz 6: Complete Steering Systems - Answer Key
1. B - The pinion rotates against the rack teeth, sliding the rack side to side to steer the wheels. [MANUAL
STEERING PRINCIPLES]

2. B - Ratio compares steering wheel input to road wheel output; higher ratios need more turns. [MANUAL
STEERING PRINCIPLES]

3. B - The pump supplies pressurised fluid that helps move the rack when the wheel is turned. [HYDRAULIC POWER
STEERING]

4. B - Low or aerated fluid starves the pump, causing noise and loss of assistance. [HYDRAULIC POWER
STEERING]

5. A - The valve senses torsion bar twist from driver effort and ports fluid to assist in that direction. [HYDRAULIC
POWER STEERING]

6. B - An electric motor drives the hydraulic pump, so assistance can be provided without the engine driving a belt
pump. [ELECTRO HYDRAULIC POWER STEERING]

7. A - Demand-based pump speed cuts parasitic load compared with a constantly driven pump. [ELECTRO
HYDRAULIC POWER STEERING]

8. B - EPS uses a motor, controlled by a module using torque sensor input, to add steering assistance. [ELECTRIC
POWER STEERING]

9. B - Torque sensor input tells the module how much assistance to apply and in which direction. [ELECTRIC
POWER STEERING]

10. B - The steering angle sensor must be recalibrated so EPS and stability systems know true straight-ahead.
[ELECTRIC POWER STEERING DIAGNOSTICS]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                               Answer Key - Quiz 6
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 7 O F 11

Quiz 7: Mastering Wheel Alignments - Answer Key
1. B - Camber is the wheel's tilt from vertical viewed from the front; top out is positive. [UNDERSTANDING STEERING
ANGLES]

2. C - Negative camber loads the inner shoulder, so that edge wears fastest. [UNDERSTANDING STEERING
ANGLES]

3. B - Positive caster helps the wheels self-centre and improves stability. [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]

4. B - Toe compares the direction of the front and rear edges of a pair of tires from above. [UNDERSTANDING
STEERING ANGLES]

5. B - Incorrect toe scrubs the tread sideways as the vehicle travels, wearing it rapidly. [UNDERSTANDING
STEERING ANGLES]

6. B - SAI is a built-in angle used diagnostically to spot bent parts when it differs side to side. [UNDERSTANDING
STEERING ANGLES]

7. B - Included angle = SAI + camber, and helps identify bent struts, knuckles or arms. [UNDERSTANDING
STEERING ANGLES]

8. B - Thrust angle is the rear toe direction relative to centreline; the vehicle tends to travel along it.
[UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]

9. B - Ackermann geometry matches each front wheel to its different turning radius, reducing scrub.
[UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]

10. B - Alignment readings are meaningless if ride height, pressures or worn parts are wrong, so these are checked
first. [UNDERSTANDING STEERING ANGLES]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                                   Answer Key - Quiz 7
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 8 O F 11

Quiz 8: Braking System Essentials - Answer Key
1. B - Friction between pad/lining and disc/drum turns motion energy into heat. [AUTOMOTIVE BRAKING
PRINCIPLES]

2. B - Pascal's principle is why pedal force at the master cylinder reaches every wheel. [AUTOMOTIVE BRAKING
PRINCIPLES]

3. B - Absorbed water drops the boiling point, risking vapour and a spongy pedal under hard braking.
[UNDERSTANDING BRAKE FLUID]

4. B - Fluids and seals are matched by specification; wrong fluid can damage rubber parts. [UNDERSTANDING
BRAKE FLUID]

5. B - Splitting the system into two circuits provides a failsafe if one circuit leaks. [BRAKE MASTER CYLINDER
OPERATION]

6. B - The port keeps the circuit filled and fully released when the pedal is up. [BRAKE MASTER CYLINDER
OPERATION]

7. B - Hydraulic pressure drives the caliper piston(s) to clamp the pads onto the disc. [DISC BRAKE SYSTEMS]

8. B - As the piston pushes the inner pad in, the sliding caliper pulls the outer pad into the disc. [DISC BRAKE
SYSTEMS]

9. B - Hydraulic pressure in the wheel cylinder pushes its pistons and the shoes into the drum. [DRUM BRAKE
SYSTEMS COMPONENTS AND OPERATIONS]

10. B - The adjuster takes up lining wear so pedal travel and parking brake action stay correct. [DRUM BRAKE
SYSTEMS CONFIGURATION AND MAINTENANCE]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                              Answer Key - Quiz 8
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 9 O F 11

Quiz 9: Advanced Braking System - Answer Key
1. B - As weight transfers forward, the rears need less pressure; the valve reduces it to avoid lockup. [HYDRAULIC
PRESSURE CONTROL AND SAFETY VALVES]

2. B - Metering holds off the front discs briefly so front and rear brakes apply together. [HYDRAULIC PRESSURE
CONTROL AND SAFETY VALVES]

3. B - A piston shifts when one circuit loses pressure and operates the warning lamp switch. [HYDRAULIC
PRESSURE CONTROL AND SAFETY VALVES]

4. B - Many vehicles combine those three valve functions in a single combination valve. [HYDRAULIC PRESSURE
CONTROL AND SAFETY VALVES]

5. A - Excess rear pressure lets the lightly loaded rear wheels lock and skid first. [HYDRAULIC PRESSURE CONTROL
AND SAFETY VALVES]

6. B - Vacuum-suspended means vacuum acts on both sides at rest; applying the pedal admits air to one side to
create assist. [BRAKE BOOSTER VACUUM SUSPENDED]

7. B - The pressure difference across the diaphragm provides the extra push on the master cylinder. [BRAKE
BOOSTER VACUUM SUSPENDED]

8. B - Without stored vacuum the booster cannot assist, so pedal effort rises sharply. [BRAKE BOOSTER VACUUM
SUSPENDED]

9. B - Hissing with poor assist points to a booster air leak or diaphragm fault. [BRAKE BOOSTER VACUUM
SUSPENDED]

10. B - The leak loses assist and upsets engine vacuum, so idle can suffer too. [BRAKE BOOSTER VACUUM
SUSPENDED]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                           Answer Key - Quiz 9
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 1 0 O F 11

Quiz 10: ABS Operations and Testing - Answer Key
1. B - By modulating pressure to a wheel about to lock, ABS preserves steering ability. [ANTI-LOCK BRAKES]

2. B - ABS cycles pressure - hold, release, reapply - many times per second to keep the wheel near peak grip.
[ANTI-LOCK BRAKES]

3. B - Pulsation is expected during ABS operation; the driver should keep firm pedal pressure. [ANTI-LOCK
BRAKES]

4. B - Passive sensors produce an AC signal that grows in frequency and voltage as speed increases. [WHEEL
SPEED SENSOR OPERATION AND TESTING]

5. B - Active sensors are supplied with power and can detect very low and even directional wheel speed. [WHEEL
SPEED SENSOR OPERATION AND TESTING]

6. B - Too large a gap or missing teeth weakens/interrupts the signal, worst at low wheel speed. [WHEEL SPEED
SENSOR OPERATION AND TESTING]

7. B - Circuit testing - resistance, continuity and wiring checks - confirms an open before parts are replaced.
[WHEEL SPEED SENSOR CIRCUIT FAULT]

8. B - Movement-related dropouts point to intermittent connections, found by wiggling the harness while watching
live data or a scope. [WHEEL SPEED SENSOR CIRCUIT FAULT]

9. B - The pump restores the pressure that the release solenoids dumped so braking can be reapplied. [ABS PUMP
MOTOR CIRCUIT DIAGNOSTICS]

10. B - A no-run pump is diagnosed electrically: feed, ground, relay control and the motor itself. [ABS PUMP MOTOR
CIRCUIT DIAGNOSTICS]

Chassis Pop Quizzes - Practice Material                                                             Answer Key - Quiz 10
A N S W E R K E Y - Q U I Z 11 O F 11

Quiz 11: Park Brake Technology - Answer Key
1. B - A motor and spindle mechanism in the caliper drives the piston to apply the pads mechanically. [CALIPER
TYPE ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE]

2. B - Service mode winds the motor back safely; forcing it can damage the mechanism. [CALIPER TYPE ELECTRIC
PARK BRAKE]

3. B - A calibration cycle sets the piston travel and confirms correct apply and release. [CALIPER TYPE ELECTRIC
PARK BRAKE]

4. B - Auto-apply uses programmed conditions to set the brake without the driver pulling the switch. [CALIPER TYPE
ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE]

5. B - One motorised actuator tensions the existing cables to apply drum or caliper parking brakes. [CABLE
ACUTED ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE]

6. B - Cable condition decides how evenly actuator force reaches each wheel. [CABLE ACUTED ELECTRIC PARK
BRAKE]

7. B - The real test is whether the vehicle stays held on a slope on the park brake alone. [CABLE ACUTED
ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE]

8. B - Too slack gives weak holding; too tight leaves the brakes dragging and overheating. [CABLE ACUTED
ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE ADJUSTMENT]

9. A - Dragging means the brake is not fully releasing, commonly from over-tight or seized cables. [CABLE ACUTED
ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE ADJUSTMENT]

10. B - Cycling settles the cables, so adjustment and release are rechecked before the job is finished. [CABLE
ACUTED ELECTRIC PARK BRAKE ADJUSTMENT]
